creative.body:
If your doctor put you on Ozempic and then told you to just take Miralax for the constipation, please read this before you buy another bottle.

I know Miralax works.

That's not the argument I'm making. I took it for 8 months. I drank the powder. I waited 12 hours. I went.

The problem wasn't that it didn't work.

The problem was that I couldn't stop taking it. The minute I skipped a day, I was right back to where I started. 7 days. 9 days. Once, 11. Like Miralax had only ever been holding the door open, and the second I let go, the door slammed shut again.

I want to talk about that door.

But first I want to tell you about the cashier at Walgreens on Hemlock.

I had a Tuesday route by the third month. 9pm, after Roy had gone to bed. Walgreens parking lot mostly empty. Aisle 3, three places down from the pharmacy. Same orange box. Same off-white powder. Same 30-day supply that would last me 14 days because I had already started doubling.

By bottle number 4 the cashier knew my face.

By bottle number 7 she had stopped asking me how my day was.

By bottle number 12 I would set the box on the counter and she would scan it without looking up. The whole transaction took 40 seconds. I would walk back across the parking lot with the bag. The plastic crinkling against my leg. The bottle in the passenger seat for the drive home.

By bottle number 16 something else had started happening, and that is the part I want you to read carefully.

The Miralax was not working as well as it had been working in month 2.

I was still taking 2 capfuls a day, the dose my GI had said was perfectly safe to stay on indefinitely. But I had started waking up on day 2 of skipping it with a stomach already getting hard by 10am. By day 3 I could not button my jeans. By day 4 I was right back in the parking lot.

The window between bottles was getting shorter.

My body was getting used to it.

I knew what that meant because I had watched it happen to my mother.

My mother took daily laxatives for 22 years. Started at 51. By 67 she had stopped going to restaurants. Her last decade was 4 walls and a bathroom routine that took 2 hours every morning. By the end her bowels would not move on their own at all. The medical term, the one nobody in my family ever said out loud, was laxative dependency.

I was 58. I was on bottle 16. I was 8 months in.

I had become the first chapter of my mother's story.

I went back to my regular GI 3 days after bottle 16. I told her I had been on Miralax for 8 months. I told her I had started doubling. I told her my body was getting used to it. I told her I was scared.

She said, "Most patients on GLP-1s don't get off it. You can stay on both indefinitely. It's perfectly safe."

I drove home with another bottle in the passenger seat.

I did not take it. I left it on the counter for 4 days and stared at it.

A friend in my book club had been through 4 GIs in 2 years before she found one who actually listened. She gave me a name. Dr. Lena Park. 50 minutes north. 6-week wait.

I took the appointment.

Dr. Park walked in 4 minutes late. Tennis shoes under her white coat. About my age. She sat down on the rolling stool. Looked at my chart for 20 seconds. Then pushed it away from her and looked at me.

She said, "I'm going to talk to you the way I talk to my sister. Not the way I'm supposed to. Is that okay?"

I said yes.

She asked me to walk her through what I had been taking and for how long. I told her. She listened the entire time without writing anything down. When I got to bottle 16 she nodded once.

She said, "Your old doctor isn't lying to you. She's leaving out half of what the medication is doing."

She let that sit there. I did not know what to do with it yet. So she kept going, in small pieces.

A few minutes later, after I had described the doubling, she said, "Miralax pulls water into your colon. There's nothing in your colon to pull water into."

She said it like that. One sentence. Then she let me chew on it.

She had me describe my 4pm pressure, the way my abdomen felt by dinner, the bloating that started on day 2 of skipping a dose. While I was talking she watched me, not the chart.

When I was done she said, "You're not constipated. You're backed up at the top. Those are 2 different things."

That was it. 4 short sentences across a 30-minute appointment. She did not lecture me. She did not pull up a diagram. She let me sit with each one until my own brain started filling in the spaces between them.

By the time I walked out to my car, the picture had assembled itself in my own head.

Here is the picture.

The medication is doing 2 separate things to my body. Not 1.

The first one is happening in my brain. The appetite suppression. The part making me eat less. That is the engine of my weight loss. The 41 pounds. The jeans. The knees. I do not want to undo that part.

The second one is happening in my stomach. Not my colon. My stomach. The medication has taken my stomach from normal to nearly frozen. Food that should leave in 4 hours is sitting there for 10 or 12. While it sits there, bacteria ferment it. That is where every symptom I have been suffering through is coming from. The bloating. The 4pm pressure. The feeling of food rotting inside me. All of it is happening 6 feet upstream from where Miralax works.

Now back to the door.

I said in the lead that Miralax is a door propped open. Here is what I mean by that, now that I understand the rest.

My stomach is the door. The medication has slammed it shut. Miralax does not touch the door. Miralax operates in a different room entirely. What Miralax does is wedge a chair against a different door, the colon door, 6 feet downstream, and force water through. As long as the chair is wedged, water moves. The minute you pull the chair out, that door slams shut too, because the original door, the stomach door, is still slammed shut from the medication.

It is not the chair's fault. The chair was never built for the stomach door.

Every product my old GI had told me to take. The Miralax. The Colace. The magnesium. The fiber. Every single one was a chair against the wrong door.

And every week I kept wedging that chair, my body was forgetting how to open the right door on its own.

That is what laxative dependency is. That is what was happening to me at bottle 16. That is what happened to my mother over 22 years.

I drove home from Dr. Park's office with no bottle in the passenger seat. First time in 8 months.

I had asked her on the way out what she would do if she were me. She had said her sister-in-law had been on a small company called Motilli for 5 months. Off Miralax for 4 of those. Standardized apigenin extract from celery, not powder. Chlorophyllin. A small targeted dose of soluble prebiotic. 90-day guarantee. She said she could not recommend it in the room. She would text me the name from the parking lot.

By the time I got to my car my phone had buzzed.

I ordered it that night.

Days 1 through 4 nothing. Day 5 the 4pm pressure was not as sharp. Day 9 I went on my own with no Miralax. By week 4 the Miralax, Colace, magnesium, fiber gummies, and psyllium husk had gone in a trash bag, and at week 6 Roy walked into the kitchen, saw the empty counter, and said, "Took you long enough."

I am not affiliated with the company.

Motilli runs a 90-day money-back guarantee. The bottles sell out for stretches because apigenin degrades from light and heat, so they batch-produce. If you have a vacation, a holiday, a wedding coming up, I would not wait until next week.

If your Miralax bottle says "do not use for more than 7 days" and you have been on it for 6 weeks, 8 months, 18 months, your body is telling you something your doctor is not. The window between bottles is getting shorter for a reason. Apigenin works on the right organ. Every product on every shelf works 6 feet downstream.

P.S. I sent Dr. Park a thank-you card 2 months in. She wrote back on the back of an old appointment card. 3 lines. Said writing me back from her car at 7pm on a Wednesday was the best part of her week. I keep that card in the drawer next to my bed.
creative.title: The Reason Your Body Is Getting "Used To" Daily Miralax (Doctors Won't Say)
